cards.title: Define desired customer emotions before designing the experience
cards.summary: Work backwards from the feelings and behaviors you want customers to have rather than pitching a product first.
cards.use_when: Designing your store's overall experience strategy, or briefing any change to the PDP, cart, post-purchase email or packaging.
steps: Instead of starting with your product and hoping customers adopt it, define the behavioral outputs you want from your customer (reorder, review, refer, subscribe) and work backwards to the proposition and experience that will produce them.
Recall a recent purchase experience of your own, then ask three questions: what happened, how did it make me feel, what did I do about it. Use this to see how feeling drives action.
Map your store's real touchpoints (ad click, PDP, cart, confirmation email, delivery, unboxing, support) and write the intended emotion for each.
Check for imbalance: if every design choice serves business metrics like AOV or urgency, customer trust can be compromised. Consider both rational and emotional needs.
Treat this as a living exercise rather than a one-off project; experiences keep evolving.
caveats: The presenter frames this as a general CX principle, not a tested ecommerce tactic.
Urgency devices like 'only two seats left at this price' were shown as stress-inducing examples, though no ecommerce sales outcome is given.

cards.title: Put a 'customer chair' in your merchandising decisions
cards.summary: Use an explicit customer-perspective check so customer needs appear on the agenda before business metrics do.
cards.use_when: Running a weekly trading, merchandising or roadmap meeting for your store where decisions about products, promotions or site changes get made.
steps: Model the practice the presenter attributes to Amazon: an empty 'customer chair' in every meeting room representing the customer, so every decision is tested against 'would our customer like this'.
Adapt for a store team: add a standing first agenda item that states the customer impact of each decision before revenue impact.
Audit whether the customer is present at all in your leadership discussions. When the presenter asks executives for their latest board protocol, the customer is very often not even on the agenda.
When someone argues for a tactic purely on business grounds, ask what the customer feels at that moment of the journey and whether trust is affected.
Consider the side benefit the presenter notes: acting as if the customer is present also tends to make meetings more efficient.
caveats: This is a described Amazon practice, not a measured ecommerce result.
It is a cultural device rather than a metric - pair it with actual customer data.

cards.title: Assess where your store sits on the random-to-differentiated CX spectrum
cards.summary: Diagnose whether your customer experience is accidental, designed or differentiated, and budget years not quarters for the transition.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your post-purchase experience and deciding how much to invest in standardising it versus differentiating it.
steps: Classify your current state honestly. Random: interactions vary by who handles them, so ordering, delivery and support outcomes are unpredictable and the presenter says this carries unnecessary cost. Intentional: a shared vision, strategy and cross-functional commitment mean everyone can think customer first, and this is where you start getting profitable. Differentiated: everyone everywhere acts in the customer's interest and you stand apart.
Look for signs of 'random' in your own operation: inconsistent reply times, variable packaging, support answers that depend on which agent picks up the ticket.

Recognise that the presenter estimates roughly 80% of companies are random, about 15% intentional and roughly 5% differentiated, and that a journey from random to differentiated takes about eight years from scratch.
Use the diagnosis to set realistic milestones for your store rather than expecting overnight transformation.
caveats: The 80/15/5 split and the eight-year journey are the presenter's figures, not a calculation you can verify for your own store.
The fish-licensing example she calls least customer-centric is an illustrative anecdote.

cards.title: Rank what customers actually value before your product
cards.summary: Corporate attitude, ease of business and helpful support outrank product quality in customers' ranking of favourite brands.
cards.use_when: Prioritising the retention and post-purchase roadmap: which improvement to fund first in support, ease, personalisation or product.
steps: Note the presenter's reported ranking from polling customers on what favourite brands do: number one is corporate attitude and doing good, then being easy to do business with, then being helpful when there is a problem, then the attitude of the people, then personalisation.
Observe that product or service only appears around sixth place, followed by consistency - most of the top of the list is emotional and relational.

Translate this into store budget allocation: audit how much you spend developing things that are not the product, versus how much goes into making the store easier to buy from and support better when something goes wrong.
Run the same reflection on your own customers: which of those attributes would they name as your number one?
Consider that the answer may depend on your product category, so don't take the order as universal.
caveats: This ranking comes from an informal live poll, not stated ecommerce research; treat it as a heuristic.
The presenter explicitly notes importance varies by product and service.

cards.title: Use purpose and word of mouth instead of pure differentiation on product
cards.summary: Products, price and quality are hard to differentiate, so treat experience and advocacy as the competitive edge.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest for competitive advantage in a crowded product category or a store selling easily-copied goods.
steps: Accept the presenter's premise that product, service, quality and price are difficult to differentiate because copying is fast and cheap; customer experience is the part less easily replicated.
Recognise that all three - product, process and people - together create something to be experienced; experience is not a substitute for the rest.
Act on the mechanism: if a customer can get the same product elsewhere, the reason to return is the experience. Otherwise they buy where it feels better.
Invest in word of mouth, which the presenter cites as trusted more than any other form of marketing (she quotes 92% of customers trusting family and friend recommendations).

Note the market shift she describes: customers buy from companies that do good, employees want to work for them, and investors look for social impact alongside return - the presenter links doing good to 78% of advocacy. Use this as direction, not a guaranteed conversion lever.
caveats: The 78% and 92% figures are quoted by the presenter without sourcing in this session.
Doing good is argued as a commercial advantage, not proven to lift store conversion.

cards.title: Ask employees what customers think before surveying customers
cards.summary: Skip intrusive surveys and start with front-line employee judgement plus data you already hold.
cards.use_when: Setting up or rethinking your store's voice-of-customer measurement, satisfaction tracking or post-purchase feedback programme.
steps: Take the presenter's position as an opinion, not a rule: she says do not measure anything that bothers your customers, because people hate surveys, and that millions of better ways exist.
Start with your own homework: find what facts and measures you already possess that reveal the answers you want. She names Lean Six Sigma quality tools as useful here.

If you have a few employees, ask them what they think the customer thinks. They are closest to reality and will feel valued; a store's front-line support and fulfilment staff often hear the real complaints.
Before asking employees, prepare a plan for acting on their feedback, because asking and then doing nothing can break employee performance and trust.
Walk in your customers' shoes: talk to customers and ask them directly rather than sending surveys.
Do not outsource judgements that are yours - the presenter's hotel example argues that asking a guest whether the room was in good shape is something the director should have checked personally.
caveats: This directly contradicts common practice of running satisfaction surveys; the presenter positions it as opposed to many of her global colleagues.
She also warns against surveys that exist to flatter the company or to whip employees, claiming the results are rarely budgeted for or acted on.

cards.title: Map the customer journey, not your internal processes
cards.summary: Journey mapping is the core tool for seeing the experience as the customer lives it and deciding where to focus improvements.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where your post-purchase experience breaks down and deciding which fulfilment, email or support step to fix first.
steps: Adopt the presenter's distinction: customers do not experience processes, they experience a journey. If they cannot feel, hear, see or touch it, it is a process, not a journey.
Map the journey end to end from the customer's side, which gives an outside-in view of the experience they actually have, plus a realistic picture of where risk sits.
Use the map to see where to put focus where it matters most to both customers and business results, rather than fixing whatever is easiest.
Before mapping, ask how capable your current processes are of delivering the journey you want, and whether you have actually decided what service or product experience you intend to deliver is.

While mapping, run 'what if' risks and decide in advance how staff should react in difficult situations, for example giving employees checklists for a customer requesting something unusual. The presenter says the map surfaces scenarios even if they never occur.
Treat journey mapping as an ongoing management tool, not a one-time workshop output.
caveats: The presenter runs a full workshop on this; one session cannot substitute for that depth.
She frames it as a tool to answer the capability question, not a guarantee of results.

cards.title: Run the three-part CX framework: strategy, measurement, people
cards.summary: Apply a simple framework covering intended experience, journey-based measurement and the culture that enables delivery.
cards.use_when: Structuring a customer experience programme across your store's merchandising, fulfilment, support and team.
steps: Part one, strategy: answer whether you know who your customers are emotionally, what experience you want them to have, and whether everyone in the organisation knows their part in delivering that journey. Most organisations, the presenter says, have not defined the intended experience at all.

Part two, measurement: use customer journey mapping plus other measures, asking whether you measure from the customer's perspective rather than internal metrics only, and what your improvement priorities are.

Part three, people: create the culture and environment that lets people act in the customer's interest. Ask whether your people know the strategy, whether they are ambassadors of the intended experience, and how processes and people enable delivery.
Note the presenter's point that this framework still applies if you work alone in your own company.
Treat the three parts as puzzle pieces: having some without connecting them means you cannot see the picture or where the benefit is greatest.
Given how the presenter describes silo thinking as the single biggest breaker of CX strategy, ensure the three parts are linked rather than owned by separate functions.
caveats: The framework is presented as a global best-practice simplification from a partner, not validated against ecommerce performance data.
She spends roughly half a day on the strategy portion alone in her three-day trainings, so a quick pass is shallow.

cards.title: Define who your customer is, emotionally as well as demographically
cards.summary: Before deciding the experience, know customers' motivators, attitudes, values and purposes beyond your product.
cards.use_when: Building customer personas or researching buyers to inform PDP copy, post-purchase messaging and retention offers.
steps: Work through the presenter's questions for each core segment: what are their key motivators, not just around your product or service but generally; what are their attitudes towards your products; what do they value in a business relationship; and what personal purposes do they have.
Ask whether your organisation is set up to understand how you are making customers feel, not just what they buy.
Follow the sequencing logic: decide who your customer is and what you do for them before deciding what the experience should be.
Recognise the limit the presenter sets: being customer-centric does not mean always doing what the customer asks, but the experience should be good enough that word of mouth spreads.
Use the resulting understanding to shape both the intended emotion at each touchpoint and the practical choices behind them.
caveats: This is a questioning framework; the source does not prescribe specific research methods beyond walking in customers' shoes and talking to them.
The presenter notes that claiming to know your customer is common but knowing them in depth is where most organisations fall short.

cards.title: Write a customer experience strategy as an umbrella over the whole store
cards.summary: Define what you want customers to feel across the journey and translate it into principles and practical actions.
cards.use_when: Creating a documented CX strategy that governs store design, fulfilment choices, support tone and team behaviour.
steps: Separate this strategy from commercial segmentation. The presenter distinguishes a customer strategy that says which segments to target from the experience strategy that states what you want customers to feel across their whole journey with you.
Anchor it under business purpose, corporate objectives and business strategy, so the experience strategy acts as an umbrella over everything you do.
Include three elements: what the experience is - what you want customers to feel; the customer principles you live by; and what each principle translates to in practice.
Then define the actions that make the intended experience actually happen, rather than leaving it as a statement.

Use the presenter's three strategy questions as a completeness check: do you know who your customers are (emotionally), what you want their experience to be, and whether everyone knows their part in delivering it.
caveats: The presenter notes most organisations have not even defined the experience they want, and lack of clarity here makes measurement very hard.
She stresses this is not a one-off annual exercise: it keeps evolving.

cards.title: Give the CX function cross-functional ownership, led from the top
cards.summary: Customer experience is a leadership and culture question, not a marketing department job.
cards.use_when: Deciding who owns customer experience in a growing store team and how it connects across marketing, fulfilment and support.
steps: Expect the common question the presenter gets about who should be in charge, and treat 'everyone' as incomplete: there should be one owner who holds it together.
Adopt her view that mature organisations have a customer experience function working cross-functionally, like a quality function, rather than treating CX as merely an external marketing activity.

Extend the principle into operations: in a production or fulfilment setting, the people assembling and packing should act in the customer's interest through the right quality and by treating each other well, because how employees are treated tends to reflect how customers end up being treated.

Place ultimate accountability with the CEO and leadership team, since the presenter calls customer experience a leadership question, like quality, where responsibility sits with everyone in the process.
Watch for silo thinking, which she identifies as the one thing that makes or breaks a CX strategy coming to life and the source of random experiences.
caveats: This is her opinion based on consulting experience, not an ecommerce-specific study.
She answers a listener who assumed marketing owns CX: marketing only covers part of it.

cards.title: Create a shared experience vision to motivate front-line staff
cards.summary: Define what customers and employees should experience together so support staff can translate product pride into helping customers.
cards.use_when: Improving support quality, agent motivation and consistency in how your store's team handles customer problems.
steps: Start from the presenter's experience managing customer support in robotics: engineers love their products like a baby, and the shift required is translating that mindset into helping customers with the product, not just helping the product.
Create a shared, common and consistent strategy together with the team: what do we want our customers to experience, and what do we want each other to experience.

Apply the same logic to employees as to customers - what do employees need, what enables them to deliver a great experience, what motivates them - and explicitly connect employee experience to delivery of the business.
Avoid the common mistake of running employee experience separately from customer experience; the presenter says most companies disconnect the two.
Accept that this kind of mindset shift takes years, not weeks.

When customers ask for one thing but need another, rely on the culture and open processes you have built, and prepare scenario guidance from journey mapping so staff can handle such conversations without being over-scripted.
caveats: The presenter says the product-minded attitude shift takes years.
She notes she is not a sales expert, so the guidance on converting a customer to a different need is directional.

cards.title: Apply the same CX principles to B2B and less emotional categories
cards.summary: B2B buyers are still people, so journey, strategy and measurement principles carry over unchanged.
cards.use_when: Selling to businesses, public sector or any buyer where you assume customer experience is a consumer-only concern.
steps: Adopt the presenter's answer to the B2B question: there is no real difference, because whatever the organisation, you meet a human, and every customer is a person.
Reject the internal objection she reports hearing - 'we're in B2B, we don't have to think about customer experience' - since every customer still has a journey with you regardless.
Keep the same principles, methodologies and strategies, while noting her remark that B2C is somewhat more advanced in CX practice, so there may be more external examples to borrow from.
For your store, map the buying journey of the person placing the order, not just the company's procurement process, including approval steps as part of the journey.
Use the same measurement questions - intended experience, journey, customer-perspective measures, improvement priorities - even where the emotional signals differ in intensity.
caveats: The presenter's own background is B2B, so this is her assessment rather than a comparative study.
She acknowledges B2C practice leads B2B, so some adaptation may be needed for your category.

cards.title: Make experience a deliberate design, not a chance outcome
cards.summary: Experiences happen whether or not you design them, so choose the experience and process deliberately.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to standardise post-purchase touchpoints such as order confirmation, shipping updates, packaging and returns handling.
steps: Accept the presenter's premise that every customer already has an experience with you whether or not you have decided what it should be, and experiences do not happen by chance - they happen by designing them.

Choose a starting point deliberately. She cites Steve Jobs taking over Apple in 1997 when sales were in steady decline, telling employees Apple had too many products and was just hoping people would buy them, then starting with the customer experience and working backwards to the technology.
Apply the same inversion to a store: define the intended purchasing experience first, then decide the tech, tools and processes that deliver it.
Watch what others deliver in your category, because customer expectations are rising through experiences like Amazon, Airbnb and Uber, and tolerance levels erode when things just work.
Use your intended experience as the standard against which new tactics and tools are judged before adoption.
caveats: The Apple account is a historical anecdote the presenter retells, not a store case study.
She presents competition on product, price and quality as difficult, meaning experience design is where deliberate choice pays off.
